content: EMP3, or Epithelial Membrane Protein 3, is a transmembrane signaling molecule encoded by the myelin-related gene EMP3. It belongs to the peripheral myelin protein gene family PMP22, which is primarily responsible for the formation of compact myelin sheaths. While the precise functions and mechanisms of EMP3 remain unclear, it is hypothesized to have epigenetic links to certain carcinomas. EMP3 is most highly expressed in peripheral blood leukocytes compared to other tissues in the body. Structurally, the protein is characterized by four transmembrane domains and two N-linked glycosylation sites located in its first extracellular loop. Function EMP3 is a transmembrane protein involved in cell-to-cell interactions and cell proliferation. Both overexpression and silencing of EMP3 disrupt its normal gene expression, which can lead to cancer progression and formation. Based on its properties and prognostic analyses in various tumors and cancers, EMP3 appears to play a tumor-suppressor-like role by regulating differentiation, apoptosis, and the development of cancer cells. However, the detailed mechanisms underlying these effects remain to be fully elucidated. Tumorigenesis and Carcinogenesis Primary Breast Carcinomas The role of EMP3 in the development of various carcinomas is not yet fully understood. However, studies have shown that EMP3 mRNA expression levels are positively correlated with primary breast carcinomas. EMP3 mRNA is expressed at higher levels in carcinoma tissues compared to normal breast tissues. Overexpression of EMP3 is significantly associated with histological grade III, lymph node metastasis, and strong HER-2 expression. Additionally, hypermethylation of the EMP3 promoter region has been observed in approximately 35% of breast carcinoma cases. Despite this, higher EMP3 expression levels are found in patients with breast carcinomas regardless of whether the promoter region is hypermethylated or unmethylated. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), primarily caused by chronic infections with hepatitis B and C viruses, has become a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide in recent years. EMP3 expression in HCC tumor cells is higher than in normal liver tissues from similar regions. Interestingly, HCC patients with relatively lower histological grades tend to exhibit higher levels of EMP3 expression. Gene silencing (knockdown) of EMP3 has been shown to reduce cell proliferation and arrest the cell cycle, suggesting a potential tumor-suppressing role for EMP3 in HCC. Brain Cancer EMP3 plays a significant role in the progression of neuroblastomas and glioblastomas, two of the most common and aggressive types of brain cancers, both of which are associated with high mortality rates. EMP3 is proposed to act as an oncogene, with its overexpression being linked to glioblastoma (GBM) progression. Reduction of EMP3 expression in CD44-high GBM cell lines promotes apoptosis of cancer cells and inhibits tumorigenesis. In 2016, a signaling pathway involving EMP3 in glioblastoma progression was identified as the TGF-β/Smad2/3 signaling pathway. Dysregulated TGF-β signaling promotes tumorigenesis in various human cells, particularly in CD44-high glioma cells. The interaction between EMP3 and the TGF-β receptor regulates TGF-β/Smad2/3 signaling activation, ultimately suppressing cell proliferation and weakening tumorigenesis in glioblastoma. Clinical Significance The effects of EMP3 on tumor suppression remain controversial, and treatments targeting EMP3-related carcinomas have not yet been validated in humans. However, some animal experiments have demonstrated positive results in suppressing tumor tissues by modifying the EMP3 gene.
